title: How does traffic policy divide requests among pods?
checkedAgainst: kube-proxy's own code and tests at Kubernetes v1.37.1, in `model.test.ts`: the rule probabilities against `computeProbability`'s expected strings in kube-proxy's proxier_test.go and a Go run of proxier.go's formatting, and the two-endpoint chain against kube-proxy's expected output. The health-check, source-NAT and equal-weight load-balancer behaviour are read from the cited source and docs, not run; the shares that follow, and the check answers `answers.ts` computes from them, are checked only by the model's own property tests (they sum to 1 and follow each policy's rule).

answer: The load balancer weighs nodes, not pods

questions.question: Under Local, with pods placed 4, 1, 0, what share of the requests does the pod on Node 2 get, and what does each pod on Node 1 get?
questions.answer: Node 3 fails the health check, so Node 1 and Node 2 get 1/2 each. Node 2’s one pod keeps all of its 1/2; Node 1 splits its 1/2 four ways, 1/8 each. The lone pod gets 4 times as many requests.

questions.question: Under Cluster, every node’s chain lists four pods. With what probabilities do its rules match, and what share does each pod get?
questions.answer: 1/4, then 1/3, then 1/2, then always: each rule matches 1/(n−i) of the requests that reach it, so each pod gets 1/4 of what the node receives.

questions.question: Which placements of four pods on these three nodes give every pod the same share under Local?
questions.answer: Only 4, 0, 0 and 2, 2, 0, in any order of the nodes. Under Local each healthy node gets an equal share and splits it among its own pods, so the shares are even exactly when every node with pods runs the same number.

steps.title: 4 pods on three nodes behind one load balancer
steps.line: Predict: with externalTrafficPolicy Local, which pod gets the most requests?
steps.caption: A Service of type LoadBalancer: a cloud load balancer sends outside requests to the nodes, and rules that kube-proxy writes on each node hand every request to a pod. Node 1 runs 3 pods, Node 2 runs 1 and Node 3 runs none. The Service’s externalTrafficPolicy sets which pods a node may pick: under Cluster, the default, any pod in the cluster; under Local, only the pods on that node. This one is set to Local.
steps.picture: Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges; 4 labelled values.

steps.title: Under Local, each node’s rules list only its own pods
steps.line: Probabilities 1/(n−i) give each pod 1/3 of the node’s requests.
steps.caption: In iptables mode kube-proxy tries one rule per pod in order. For three pods, the first takes 1/3; the second takes half of the remaining 2/3, another 1/3; the last gets the final 1/3. In general, rule i of n matches 1/(n−i) of the requests that reach it, counting i from zero, so each pod gets 1/n. Under Local Node 1 lists only its 3 pods: 1/3, 1/2, always, so each gets 1/3 of what Node 1 receives.
steps.picture: Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges; Code, 4 lines. Note: “1/3” beside Pod a; “1/3” beside Pod b; “1/3” beside Pod c; chain shown: Node 1 · 10.240.0.1. New in this step: Code, 4 lines.

steps.title: Node 3 runs no pod, so it fails the health check
steps.line: Node 1 and Node 2 answer 200 and each get 1/2 of requests.
steps.caption: Under Local, kube-proxy answers the load balancer’s health check on each node: 200 when the node runs a pod of the Service, 503 when it runs none. The load balancer stops sending to Node 3. It divides requests equally among healthy nodes, regardless of their pod counts, so Node 1 and Node 2 each get 1/2 of the requests. The next choice happens inside each node: its share is divided among its own pods.

steps.title: Answer: pod d gets 1/2 of the requests; pods a, b and c get 1/6 each
steps.line: Split by node, not pod: each node with pods gets 1/2.
steps.caption: The load balancer weighs nodes, not pods: Node 1 and Node 2 each get 1/2. Node 1 splits its 1/2 three ways; Node 2 sends all of its 1/2 to pod d, so pod d gets 3 times as many requests as pod a.
steps.picture: Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges. Note: “16.7%” beside Pod a; “16.7%” beside Pod b; “16.7%” beside Pod c; and 1 more.

steps.title: Under Local, Node 2’s whole 1/2 flows into pod d
steps.line: Band width is share of requests; colour is the node a request enters.
steps.caption: The load balancer cuts by node; each node’s rules cut among the pods they list. Under Cluster each node’s 1/3 fans out to all 4 pods, so every pod bar collects three colours and ends at 1/4. Under Local Node 1 cuts its 1/2 into three bands of 1/6, Node 2’s whole 1/2 goes to pod d and Node 3 gets no band, so pod d’s bar ends 3 times as wide as pod a’s.
steps.picture: Cluster: bands as wide as their share of requests, from the load balancer to the nodes and on to the pods. Node 1 gets 1/3 and passes it to pod a (1/12), pod b (1/12), pod c (1/12), pod d (1/12); Node 2 gets 1/3 and passes it to pod a (1/12), pod b (1/12), pod c (1/12), pod d (1/12); Node 3 gets 1/3 and passes it to pod a (1/12), pod b (1/12), pod c (1/12), pod d (1/12). Pods end with a 25%, b 25%, c 25%, d 25%. Local: bands as wide as their share of requests, from the load balancer to the nodes and on to the pods. Node 1 gets 1/2 and passes it to pod a (1/6), pod b (1/6), pod c (1/6); Node 2 gets 1/2 and passes it to pod d (1/2); Node 3 gets no band. Pods end with a 16.7%, b 16.7%, c 16.7%, d 50%.

steps.title: The request stays on its node and keeps the client’s address
steps.line: Pod a sees 198.51.100.79: no source NAT and no second hop.
steps.caption: Node 1’s rules list only its own pods, so the request never leaves Node 1, and kube-proxy adds no source NAT for it. Pod a sees the client’s address, 198.51.100.79. Under Local no outside request takes a second hop.
steps.picture: Architecture diagram: 8 services, 7 edges. Note: “from 198.51.100.79” beside Pod a; travelled: Load balancer → Node 1 · 10.240.0.1; Node 1 · 10.240.0.1 → Pod a.

steps.title: With 3, 1, 0 pods, Local trades even load for the client’s address
steps.line: Cluster sends 2 in 3 requests to another node; Local sends none.
steps.caption: Cluster spreads requests evenly over the pods, but 2 in 3 cross to another node and every pod sees a node’s address. Local keeps each request on its node with the client’s address. The load balancer weighs nodes, not pods, so pod d takes 3 times the load of pod a.

steps.title: 3 pods on three nodes behind one load balancer
steps.line: Predict: with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster, which pod gets the most requests?
steps.caption: A Service of type LoadBalancer: a cloud load balancer sends outside requests to the nodes, and rules that kube-proxy writes on each node hand every request to a pod. Node 1 runs 1 pod, Node 2 runs 1 and Node 3 runs 1. The Service’s externalTrafficPolicy sets which pods a node may pick: under Cluster, the default, any pod in the cluster; under Local, only the pods on that node. This one is set to Cluster.
steps.picture: Architecture diagram: 7 services, 7 edges; 4 labelled values.

steps.title: Each node’s rules pick one of all 3 pods
steps.line: Probabilities 1/(n−i) give each pod 1/3 of the node’s requests.
steps.caption: In iptables mode kube-proxy tries one rule per pod in order. For three pods, the first takes 1/3; the second takes half of the remaining 2/3, another 1/3; the last gets the final 1/3. In general, rule i of n matches 1/(n−i) of the requests that reach it, counting i from zero, so each pod gets 1/n. Under Cluster every node lists all 3 pods: 1/3, 1/2, always, so each gets 1/3 of what the node receives.

steps.title: Under Cluster, 2 in 3 requests leave the node they reach
steps.line: Node 3 sends this request on to pod b on Node 2.
steps.caption: Each node gets a third of the requests and picks among all 3 pods. A request leaves its node when the pick runs elsewhere: 2 in 3 on Node 1, 2 in 3 on Node 2, 2 in 3 on Node 3. Here Node 3 sends one to pod b on Node 2.

steps.title: Answer: none. Each pod gets 1/3 of the requests
steps.line: Each node splits its 1/3 among all 3 pods.
steps.caption: The load balancer weighs nodes, not pods: it gives each node 1/3, and under Cluster each node’s rules give each of the 3 pods 1/3 of that. Summed over the three nodes, each pod gets 1/3 of all requests, wherever it runs.
